scenario: Today's embodied AI track is about making robots move faster and more reliably in real deployment. W2A uses a video model only during training to teach the action model and removes it at deployment; PTS leaves the model unchanged and simply keeps the robot moving during inference, travelling faster along the planned path. JADE has the vision-language model take part in generating actions at every denoising step, and ODE Policy builds the continuity of actions directly into the policy. Reuse across robots is another thread: PointPilot predicts how objects move instead of joint actions, and Pixel designs low-cost hardware, wearable data collection and policy learning together. ReGATE lets a humanoid still pick up a box when its camera is blocked. There is also a public dataset of real-robot failures, well suited to training reward models.

papers.title: ReGATE: Recurrent Gated Visual Fusion for Reactive Humanoid-Object Interaction
papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating object acquisition, transport, and release from onboard sensing while responding to user commands and incomplete visual observations. We present ReGATE, a whole-body controller that combines egocentric depth, proprioception, and online locomotion and contact commands. Built on a teacher-student framework, ReGATE integrates interaction-state estimation through a recurrent adapter that predicts object geometry and physical contact without an external object-pose estimator. Head-wise and global gates regulate visual updates to a proprioceptive pathway. A visual-grounding and corruption curriculum trains the adapter, while phase-aware initialization increases coverage of brief contact transitions. In simulation, ReGATE achieves 85.2% success across 330 static-object acquisition trials, compared with 48.5% for VisualMimic under the same protocol, and 85.9% across 440 moving-object acquisition trials. Deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates co
papers.summary: When a humanoid robot reaches for a box, the box blocks its head depth camera as soon as the hands get close, yet the controller still has to finish the whole sequence of picking up, carrying and putting down. This paper lets the robot act mainly through the joint-state pathway and treats the depth image only as a correction scaled by learned gates, designed to let less of it in when the image is unreliable. Information gathered over earlier frames is kept in the memory of recurrent layers, so it is not lost the moment the image drops out. In simulation it picks up static boxes 85.2% of the time, against 48.5% for VisualMimic under the same protocol. On a real Unitree G1, after the camera saw the box once and was then completely covered, the robot still grasped the box. ==When the view can be blocked, relying mainly on joint states and taking in the image as needed is steadier.==

papers.title: Pixel: A Co-Designed Full-Stack Robot System for Learning General-Purpose Mobile Manipulation
papers.authors: Tony Tao, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Deepak Pathak
papers.abstract: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body
papers.summary: In mobile-manipulation robots, the hardware, the data-collection devices, whole-body control and policy learning are usually built separately, and when they are put together they often hold each other back. This CMU paper designs all four together: a wheeled humanoid that costs under $15,000, with an upper body proportioned like a human, plus a low-cost wearable rig that lets a person record demonstrations without the robot present. Because the body proportions match, human demonstrations can teach the robot directly, and demonstrations recorded with the wearable rig alone are enough to train mobile-manipulation policies. Scored by how far each task gets completed, the full robot gets a perfect score on three ablation tasks, and disabling the torso drops the average to 47.4%, which shows the policy really uses those joints. Teams that want to build a full platform cheaply can take it as a ready starting point.

papers.title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
papers.authors: Xicheng Gong, Wenxuan Song, Chengze Liu, Qiwei Li, Qize Yu, Jiaolong Yang, Haoang Li, Yadong Mu
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to
papers.summary: In a common kind of robot model, a vision-language model looks at the images and reads the instruction, and an action module then turns noise into an action step by step through diffusion. But the vision-language model usually just gives a fixed condition at the start and takes no part in the denoising that follows. This paper finds that letting it join every denoising step makes actions more accurate in situations never seen in training. Concretely, the vision-language model reads the current noisy action at every step and passes what it reads to the action module through a gated attention layer; during training it is also asked directly to recover clean actions from noisy ones. On four real-world bimanual tasks, average success is 20.8 percentage points higher than π0.5. Denoising together also needs fewer sampling steps, which partly offsets the cost of running the vision-language model.

papers.title: W2A: Distilling World Priors into Action Models for Real-Time Robotic Control
papers.authors: Xiaopeng Zhang, Yongjin Mu, Yueyang Weng, Chengzhi Zhao, Yanjie Li
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently shown great promise in robotic control, benefiting from the future imagination capability of large-scale pretrained video models. However, most existing WAMs require explicitly imagining future states at test time, incurring substantial computational overhead and latency that make them unsuitable for real-time robotic control. In this paper, we propose W2A, a two-stage distillation framework for real-time robotic manipulation that distills intermediate denoising representations from a video diffusion model into an action model during training, while entirely discarding the video model at test time. We hypothesize that although video latent representations are high-dimensional, a compressed low-dimensional subspace is sufficient to provide effective supervision for action generation. This makes it possible to transfer such information effectively into an action model. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate co
papers.summary: Letting a robot first predict the next few video frames and then choose an action makes the policy understand physics better, but every control step then has to run a video model, which is too slow for real-time control. This paper uses the video model only during training. It first uses PCA to compress the video diffusion model's intermediate representations into a few dimensions, then adds a training loss that makes the action model's own intermediate representations match this compressed version. At deployment the video model is removed entirely. The authors' hypothesis is that although video representations are high-dimensional, the information that actually matters for actions fits in a much smaller subspace. On LIBERO it reaches 95.9% average success, with inference about 21 times faster than a representative model that predicts frames before acting. ==Knowledge from video pretraining can be taught to the action model during training, so inference no longer pays for it.==

papers.title: Rollout then Recycle: 3,718 Labelled Real-Robot Episodes from Benchmarking 7 Policies on 12 Tasks
papers.authors: Praveen Selvaraj, Lorenzo Uttini, Ville Kuosmanen
papers.abstract: We release all 3,718 episodes from the ArmnetBench v0.1 evaluation (arXiv:2607.24481), which contains 600 teleoperated demonstrations and 3,118 rollouts of seven imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies on 12 tabletop tasks, recorded on low-cost SO-101 arms; 73% of the rollouts are failures. Every policy for a task was trained or fine-tuned on the same 50 demonstrations and rolled out on the same cell, so the corpus contains many policies' failures on shared tasks. An operator labelled every rollout successful, suboptimal or failure. Each episode has three camera views, joint states and actions and is available on the Hugging Face Hub in LeRobot v3.0 and a reward-model format. This note documents how the episodes were collected and the limitations that could affect their use.
papers.summary: Every robot benchmark produces many failure recordings, yet large public datasets are almost all successful demonstrations. This paper releases all 3,718 episodes from the ArmnetBench evaluation; besides the teleoperated demonstrations, most are rollouts of 7 imitation-learning and VLA policies on 12 tabletop tasks. 73% of the rollouts are failures. Every policy for a task was trained on the same set of demonstrations and run on the same low-cost arm setup, and an operator labelled each rollout as successful, achieved with a poor finish, or failed. So on the same task one can see how many different policies fail in their own ways. Teams that want to train reward models or build failure detection finally have a sizeable, labelled set of real-robot failures.

papers.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
papers.authors: Jindou Jia, Jingliang Li, Kuangji Zuo, Tuo An, Yuxuan Hu, Mengfei Zhao, Bofan Lyu, Jiaqi Bai, Daoyuan Zhu, Hengyu Dai, Junpeng Zhang, Jianfei Yang
papers.abstract: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL
papers.summary: Most robot policies output an action value directly at each control step, and whether consecutive actions connect smoothly is left for the model to learn. This paper instead learns how the action changes: a neural ordinary differential equation learns the direction in which the action moves over time, and at deployment each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. The same situation often allows several valid moves, such as passing an obstacle on the left or the right, and learning only the average direction drives straight into it. So at the start of each chunk, a small module samples an offset from a few learned candidate directions, one per way around; every step of that chunk adds this offset to the direction of change, so the whole chunk follows one route. In imitation learning after one training epoch, its success rate is 5.9 times that of the common flow-matching policy and it generates actions 10.8 times faster; on 14 real-world tasks it has the highest success rate.

papers.title: Same Path, Less Time: Training-Free Fast Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models under Inference Latency
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, yet deployed robots waste time in two ways that are independent of model capability: they halt while the next chunk is inferred, and they move at the speed of slow, cautious demonstrations. Existing remedies remove one loss each, and stacking them fails, because asynchrony and speed-up each change the correspondence between planned progress and executed motion. We present Path-preserving Time Scaling (PTS), a training-free execution layer for frozen action-chunking policies built on one principle: the robot's motion is a time reparameterization of a reference path, and the path changes only in response to new observations. A path layer decodes every replan deterministically in one step and enters it at the progress consumed during inference. A time layer sums the planned increments, keeps the arm at 1x while the gripper moves, and caps the rate by the actuator's linear range and by chunk feasibility under latency. We
papers.summary: Deployed robots waste time in two ways: they stop while the model computes the next chunk of actions, and they move at the careful, slow speed of human demonstrations. This paper changes neither the model nor its training, only how actions are executed. The robot follows the path the policy planned but moves along it faster, and the path is updated only when a new observation arrives. The gripper keeps its original speed, and the speed-up is capped by the motors' capability and the inference latency. On LIBERO with injected inference latency, task throughput is 33% higher than the strongest deployable baseline for π0.5 and 104% higher for SmolVLA, with equal or better success. ==The losses from pausing and slow motion can be recovered without touching the model.==

papers.title: PointPilot: Unified Robotic Manipulation via Object-Centric 3D Point Flow Prediction
papers.authors: Yihan Fang, Yuxin Tian, Ruixiang Wang, Zhanqi Zhang, Xing Hu, Zhen Yang, Huayi Zhou, Yongyi Su, Wei Gao, Kui Jia
papers.abstract: Generalization remains a central challenge in robotics, calling for policies that address domain variations from multiple dimensions such as diverse embodiments, camera poses, and/or scene layouts. In order to approach this problem, we introduce PointPilot, a task-focused and 3D aligned manipulation framework built on a 3D space point-flow prediction. Rather than modeling the global scene, PointPilot only represents task-focused objects (robot grippers treated as objects), avoiding the prediction of potentially redundant scene parts unrelated to the manipulation tasks. Moreover, PointPilot aligns 3D spatial representation in one unified coordinate and supports closed-loop and fully automatic action execution across different manipulation modes from object point flow without a separately trained action expert, while existing works typically need an extra action head or are (semi-)automatic and single-arm mode specific. Given sensor observations and language instructions, our model joint
papers.summary: Different robots have different action formats, so mixed demonstration data is hard to use as one kind of supervision. This paper changes what is predicted. Instead of joint actions, it predicts how points on the task-relevant objects move in 3D space, treating the robot's gripper as one of the objects. Execution needs no trained module. Before grasping, the gripper follows the predicted motion of its own points. After grasping, the object and gripper are treated as one rigid body. A rotation plus translation is fitted from the current and predicted positions of the object's points and applied to the gripper's pose, and each robot's own controller carries it out. Because the supervision does not depend on the robot model, demonstrations from different robots can be trained together. In RoboTwin simulation, a policy trained only on ALOHA data was deployed without fine-tuning on ARX and Piper arms it had never seen. ==Predicting how objects move transfers across robots more easily than predicting how joints move.==

papers.title: Simulate, train, and operate robots with Google Cloud physical AI
papers.abstract: Today, we are sharing how Google Cloud physical AI brings simulation, model training, and real-world deployment together on one platform for robotics developers and engineering teams.
papers.summary: A robotics team developing a policy usually switches tools between simulation, model training and real-robot deployment, moving data and models across several systems. This Google Cloud blog post introduces its physical AI offering for robot developers, which puts simulation, model training and real-world deployment on one cloud platform. It is not a new algorithm; its value is in connecting the stages: when the whole workflow runs on one platform, the turnaround from training in simulation to running on a real robot gets shorter. Whether it is worth migrating depends on a team's existing toolchain and the cost of cloud compute.

papers.title: AgiBot "AI WAVE" launches seven new releases in a row, with a full technology stack putting robots to work
papers.abstract: As a prelude to and extension of AgiBot Innovation Day 2026, starting October 22 AgiBot launches "AI WAVE", releasing seven results in a row: a dataset, a work platform, a robot body, an agent framework, a simulation platform, a foundation model and a collective experience learning paradigm, showing its full-stack embodied AI technology.
papers.summary: In late October AgiBot released seven results over seven days, covering a dataset, a work platform, a heavy-duty robot, an agent framework, a simulation platform, a foundation model and collective experience learning. It then sent 6 G2 robots into a real convenience store for a 24-hour livestream of stocking, restocking and making hot food. Its claim is that deploying robots needs the whole technology stack working together, and a single strong model is not enough. Its simulation platform claims over 95% consistency between real-robot and simulated results on complex tasks. This is a vendor announcement with no evaluation method given; but putting robots on continuous shifts in a real store exposes long-running problems better than a one-off demo.
